subTopics.name: How do we understand and measure Australia’s health?

dotPoints.description: Compare meanings of health, using various sources, including the World Health Organization’s (WHO) definition, and explain why people give different meanings to health

prompts.question: Outline the World Health Organization (WHO) definition of health, and one different meaning of health from another source.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class is preparing a presentation on how different sources define health. Students have the WHO definition and the Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion (1986) to compare.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the WHO definition of health and a different meaning of health from another named source, with accurate detail
2 marks: Outlines the WHO definition of health OR one different meaning of health from another source
1 mark: Identifies a relevant meaning of health without a named source
markerNotes: Full marks need the WHO definition stated accurately, plus a second meaning of health from a named source, so that the answer shows the meanings differ.
Accept any accurate second source, such as the Ottawa Charter, provided its meaning of health is explained rather than only named.
A paraphrase of the WHO definition earns credit only if it keeps the physical, mental and social dimensions.
commonStudentErrors: States that the WHO defines health only as the absence of disease, which leaves out the mental and social dimensions.
Gives two meanings from the same source, so no different meaning from another source is outlined.
Writes a general definition of health from memory without linking it to a named source.

sampleAnswers.answer: The World Health Organization (WHO) definition describes health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. Another source, the Ottawa Charter, offers a different meaning of health, describing it as a resource for everyday life rather than the objective of living. These two sources show that people use different meanings of health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the WHO definition and a different meaning from a named source with accurate detail, which meets the 3-mark row. Both meanings are stated clearly, so the comparison is visible to the marker.

sampleAnswers.answer: The WHO defines health as complete physical, mental and social well-being. This is one meaning, but the answer gives no second meaning from another source.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the WHO definition accurately but gives no second meaning from another source, which meets the 2-mark row. A named second source would reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Health means feeling well and being free from illness.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives a relevant meaning of health without naming a source, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Explain why these two students give different meanings of health, referring to the circumstances that shape each view.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two students in the same Year 11 class give different answers when asked what health means to them. One has lived with asthma since childhood and says health means being able to play sport. The other works part time while studying and says health means having enough sleep and money to pay the bills.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains thoroughly why people give different meanings of health, linking specific circumstances in the scenario to each student's view
4 marks: Explains why people give different meanings of health, with relevant links to both students
3 marks: Explains one reason why people give different meanings of health, with some links to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a reason why people give different meanings of health, with a limited link to the scenario
1 mark: Identifies a factor that may affect a person's meaning of health
markerNotes: Strong answers explain the mechanism: a circumstance shapes what a person notices or values about their health.
Link each explanation to a student in the scenario rather than giving general reasons alone.
Culture, age and socioeconomic situation are credited when they are explained, not merely listed.
commonStudentErrors: Describes what each student values without explaining why their circumstances shape that value.
Says people just have different opinions, without giving a reason for the difference.
Treats the WHO definition as the only correct meaning of health rather than one meaning among several.

sampleAnswers.answer: People give different meanings of health because their life experiences, circumstances and personal values shape what they see as important for wellbeing. The first student has lived with asthma since childhood, so being able to play sport is a visible sign of good health for them, reflecting a long-term experience of a chronic condition. The second student works part time while studying, so sleep and money matter because they affect daily functioning and stress. Culture, age and socioeconomic situation can also shape these meanings of health, which is why a broad definition such as the WHO one can be accepted in principle but applied differently by each person.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains why meanings differ by linking each student's circumstances to their view of health, which meets the 5-mark row. The explanation is widened to culture, age and socioeconomic situation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Different people have different life experiences, so they value different things. The student with asthma values sport, while the student who works values sleep and money. Culture and age could also change what health means.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains one reason for different meanings and links it to both students, which meets the 3-mark row. How circumstances shape each view is brief, and culture and age are only named.

sampleAnswers.answer: Some people think health is about being fit, and others think it is about money.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a factor that may affect a person's meaning of health with no explanation of why, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Explain the dynamic nature of health by exploring the interactions between the dimensions of health, the concept of good health, the health continuum, how health changes over time, and how an individual’s circumstances affect their health

prompts.question: Describe the health continuum, and use Sam's experience to show how health changes over time.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Sam had a sports injury last year that limited training for several months. Sam's physical health improved during recovery, but Sam felt less connected to friends and found it harder to concentrate at school.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the health continuum and at least two dimensions of health, with an accurate example of health changing over time
2 marks: Describes the health continuum OR the dimensions of health, with some relevant detail
1 mark: Identifies a dimension of health or a point on the continuum
markerNotes: The top row needs the continuum described as a range, not as a list of terms, plus an example that shows change.
Credit any accurate dimension of health, such as physical, mental or social, as long as the example uses it.
The top row expects the answer to show the dimensions changing separately, not only one dimension changing.
commonStudentErrors: Treats the health continuum as only two states, healthy and unhealthy, with no range in between.
Lists dimensions of health without linking any of them to Sam's experience.
Says health is only physical, ignoring the mental and social dimensions.

sampleAnswers.answer: The health continuum is a range from ill health to good health, and a person can move along it at different times. The dimensions of health, such as physical health and social health, can change separately: Sam's physical health improved during recovery, while Sam's social health declined as contact with friends fell. This shows how health changes over time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the continuum as a range and gives two dimensions of health that change separately, which meets the 3-mark row. The example is accurate and tied to Sam.

sampleAnswers.answer: The health continuum runs from ill health to good health. Sam's injury moved Sam towards the ill health end for a time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the continuum with a link to Sam, which meets the 2-mark row. Naming and explaining a dimension of health would reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Physical health is one dimension of health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one dimension of health without describing it or giving an example, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse how interactions between the dimensions of health show the dynamic nature of health, using Maria's circumstances.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Maria, aged 17, moved interstate for her final year of school. She lost her regular sport and close friends, began sleeping poorly, and felt anxious about her studies.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the dimensions of health interact and change over time, with detailed links to Maria's circumstances showing that health is dynamic
5 marks: Analyses how the dimensions of health interact, with relevant links to Maria's circumstances
4 marks: Explains how the dimensions of health affect each other, with some links to Maria's circumstances
3 marks: Describes a dimension of health and how Maria's circumstances affect it
2 marks: Identifies a change in Maria's circumstances, with a limited link to health
1 mark: Identifies a dimension of health or a point on the continuum
markerNotes: The top row needs the interactions shown as a chain of cause and effect over time, not as a list of dimensions.
A strong answer shows how one change in circumstances shifts more than one dimension of health at once.
Credit a student who notes that health can improve again, because this shows health is dynamic rather than fixed.
commonStudentErrors: Treats the dimensions of health as separate boxes, so no interaction between them is explained.
Describes Maria's problems without placing them on the health continuum.
Says health is fixed once a person becomes unwell, which contradicts the dynamic nature of health.

sampleAnswers.answer: Health is dynamic because it changes over time and across the dimensions of health, which interact rather than operating separately. Maria's loss of regular sport affects her physical health, while losing close friends affects her social health. Poor sleep then links the physical and mental dimensions, since tiredness makes anxiety about her studies harder to manage. Her mental health therefore moves towards the ill health end of the health continuum before any physical change is visible. Her circumstances, including a new school and separation from her support network, show that a person's position on the continuum can shift quickly. Good health is not a fixed state, so Maria's health can improve again if she rebuilds friendships, returns to activity and gets enough sleep. This shows that the dynamic nature of health depends on how the dimensions of health interact with circumstances over time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the interactions over time, with detailed links to Maria's circumstances, which meets the 6-mark row. The answer also shows that health can move back along the continuum, so health is seen as dynamic.

sampleAnswers.answer: Health changes over time because the dimensions of health affect each other. Maria losing sport affects her physical health, and losing friends affects her social health. Her poor sleep and anxiety link to her mental health, so her health moves along the continuum.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how the dimensions of health affect each other, with some links to Maria's circumstances, which meets the 4-mark row. The answer does not show the change building over time or how health can improve again.

sampleAnswers.answer: Maria lost her sport and friends after moving, which may affect her health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a change in Maria's circumstances with a limited link to health, which meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Discuss the use of epidemiology, mortality, infant mortality, morbidity, incidence and prevalence to explain the health status of Australians using tables and graphs from Australia’s Health and other health reports

prompts.question: Calculate the mortality rate per 100 000 people and the infant mortality rate per 1000 live births for the region in the scenario, showing your working.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A health report for a region with a population of 250 000 records 1 500 deaths in one year, including 40 deaths of infants under one year old. The region had 4 200 live births in the same year.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Calculates both rates correctly, with working and units shown for each
2 marks: Calculates one rate correctly, or calculates both with an error in the working
1 mark: Identifies the formula for one of the rates
markerNotes: Full marks need both rates, each with its formula, the values from the scenario and units such as deaths per 100 000 people.
Credit correct arithmetic with slightly different rounding, such as 9.52 rather than 9.5 deaths per 1 000 live births.
Working must use the figures in the scenario, so a rate recalled from memory earns no credit.
commonStudentErrors: Divides deaths by population without multiplying by 100 000, so the answer is a proportion rather than a rate.
Uses all births rather than live births as the denominator for the infant mortality rate.
Gives the infant mortality rate per 100 000 live births, which does not match the unit the question asks for.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mortality rate = number of deaths ÷ population × 100 000 = 1 500 ÷ 250 000 × 100 000 = 600 deaths per 100 000 people. Infant mortality rate = infant deaths ÷ live births × 1 000 = 40 ÷ 4 200 × 1 000 = 9.5 deaths per 1 000 live births. Rates standardise counts so that populations of different sizes can be compared.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates both rates with the formula, working and units shown, which meets the 3-mark row. The closing sentence explains why rates are used rather than raw counts.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mortality rate = 1 500 ÷ 250 000 × 100 000 = 600 deaths per 100 000 people, so the overall death rate for the region is known.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the mortality rate correctly with units, which meets the 2-mark row. The infant mortality rate is not calculated, so the answer cannot reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mortality rate = number of deaths ÷ population × 100 000.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives the formula for one rate without calculating it, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Discuss how epidemiology, including incidence, prevalence and morbidity, helps explain the health status of Australians shown in tables and graphs from health reports.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A table in a health report shows that asthma prevalence among children is higher in one region than the national average, while the incidence of new diagnoses in that region has fallen over five years.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how incidence, prevalence and morbidity together explain health status, using the trends in the tables and graphs and noting the limits of the data
5 marks: Discusses how these measures explain health status, with relevant use of the data in the scenario
4 marks: Explains how two measures describe health status, with some reference to the data
3 marks: Describes epidemiological measures with a limited link to the scenario
2 marks: Defines one or two measures without applying them to the data
1 mark: Identifies a measure used in epidemiology
markerNotes: Strong answers use the paired trend in the scenario, lower incidence with higher prevalence, to show what the measures do and do not reveal.
Credit an interpretation that considers how long people live with a condition, since prevalence captures that duration.
A list of definitions with no reference to the table earns no more than the 2-mark row.
commonStudentErrors: Treats prevalence and incidence as the same measure, so the trend is misread.
Reads higher prevalence as proof that more people became unwell, without considering the rate of new cases.
Uses death counts to judge how common an illness is, rather than morbidity or prevalence measures.

sampleAnswers.answer: Epidemiology uses measures such as incidence, prevalence and morbidity to describe the health status of a population. Incidence counts new cases over a period, so a falling incidence suggests fewer people are developing the condition. Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point in time, so it reflects both new cases and people living with the condition for longer. Morbidity describes the level of illness in a population, not only deaths. The scenario shows higher prevalence alongside falling incidence, which may mean people are living longer with asthma or that existing cases are well managed, rather than that more people are becoming unwell. Tables and graphs from health reports, such as Australia's Health, allow these measures to be compared across regions and over time, but they need careful interpretation. The data cannot show why a trend occurs without considering access to care, diagnosis and the environment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses the three measures together and uses the paired trend in the scenario to show what they reveal and what they do not, which meets the 6-mark row. The limits of the data are noted.

sampleAnswers.answer: Epidemiology measures such as incidence and prevalence describe the health status of a population. In the scenario, prevalence is higher in one region, but incidence has fallen, so more people are living with asthma. Morbidity shows how much illness there is. Health reports help compare regions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how two measures describe health status and refers to the scenario, which meets the 4-mark row. It does not explain why the pair of trends may mislead, so it stops short of the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Prevalence is the number of existing cases, and incidence is the number of new cases.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines two measures without applying them to the data, which meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Investigate the role of social justice principles, participation, equity, access and rights, in promoting an individual and community’s health status

prompts.question: Outline how equity and access to services can improve the health status of the community in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A rural town has one general practice that is open two days a week, and residents must travel about 90 minutes to reach the nearest hospital. The local council plans to extend clinic hours and add a telehealth service, and it will hold public meetings so residents can help plan the changes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines how equity and access improve the health status of the community, with specific links to the scenario and to participation
2 marks: Outlines one way equity or access improves health, with a link to the scenario
1 mark: Identifies a social justice principle relevant to health
markerNotes: Full marks need equity and access applied to the town, not defined in general terms.
Credit the link between participation and services that match local needs, since the scenario gives residents a say.
A definition of social justice on its own earns only the 1-mark row.
commonStudentErrors: Defines equity as treating everyone the same, without linking fair distribution to need.
Describes the town's problems without stating how the proposed changes would improve health status.
Mentions participation without explaining how it leads to better services or health.

sampleAnswers.answer: Equity means health services are provided according to need, so a town with few services needs extra support to reach the same health status as other communities. Extended clinic hours and a telehealth service improve access for residents who cannot easily travel 90 minutes to hospital. Community participation in the public meetings lets residents help shape services that meet local needs, which supports social justice principles in promoting health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines how equity and access improve health status for the town, with links to the scenario and to participation, which meets the 3-mark row. Each principle is applied to the town rather than defined in general.

sampleAnswers.answer: Extended clinic hours will help residents see a doctor when they need one, which improves their access to health services.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines one way access improves health, linked to the scenario, which meets the 2-mark row. Adding equity or participation would reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Social justice principles include equity and access.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies relevant principles without explaining how they affect health, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Assess the extent to which social justice principles of participation, equity, access and rights promote the health status of individuals and communities in Australia.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A council is deciding whether to fund a free program that helps Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families use local health services. Some residents see it as a community responsibility, while others argue that access to health care is a right for every resident.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the extent to which the principles promote health status, weighing strengths and limitations with sustained judgement supported by detailed links to the scenario
5 marks: Assesses how the principles promote health status, with a clear judgement and relevant links to the scenario
4 marks: Explains how two or more principles affect health status, with some link to the scenario
3 marks: Describes a social justice principle and its effect on health status, with a limited link to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a social justice principle with a basic link to health
1 mark: Identifies a principle relevant to health status
markerNotes: The top row needs a judgement on the extent of the effect, with the strengths and limits of each principle weighed against the scenario.
Credit a student who argues that the principles work best together, such as participation shaping how access is delivered.
Equity and rights are not interchangeable; credit answers that keep the two distinct.
commonStudentErrors: Lists the four principles without judging how far each one promotes health status.
Says social justice always improves health, without acknowledging limits such as funding or tokenistic consultation.
Treats access and equity as the same principle rather than explaining how they differ.

sampleAnswers.answer: Social justice principles promote health status to a substantial extent when they are put into practice, but their effect depends on how they are applied. Equity is strongest where resources go to groups with the greatest need, such as the free program that helps families use services. Access improves when cost, distance and cultural safety barriers are reduced, so more people use preventive care earlier. Participation strengthens these effects because communities that help plan services are more likely to trust and use them. Rights frame health as an entitlement, and the WHO Constitution describes the highest attainable standard of health as a fundamental right of every human being. However, rights alone do not change outcomes if services are underfunded or hard to reach, and participation can be tokenistic when community views do not shape decisions. Overall, the principles promote health status considerably where they are backed by funding and genuine consultation, but only partly when they remain statements of intent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses the extent of the effect with a clear judgement, weighing the strengths and limits of each principle against the scenario, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Equity and access help health status because services reach people who need them, such as the families in the scenario. Participation helps communities trust services. Rights mean everyone should be able to use health care, but this only works if it is funded.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how several principles affect health status, with links to the scenario, which meets the 4-mark row. The limits of the principles are not weighed, so no judgement is reached.

sampleAnswers.answer: Equity is a social justice principle that means fairness in health services.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a social justice principle with a basic link to health, which meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Discuss the range of determinants (broad features of society, environmental factors, socioeconomic characteristics, health behaviours and biomedical factors), that influence the health and wellbeing of Australians (how do the determinants interact to affect the health of population groups?; what are the sociological causes of risky health behaviours?; where do inequities exist and what can we do about them?)

prompts.question: Classify each of the four factors in the scenario into the determinant category it belongs to.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A health worker lists four factors that may affect residents' health in one suburb: household income, air pollution near a major road, regular smoking and a family history of heart disease.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Classifies all four factors into the correct determinant category, with a brief reason for each
3 marks: Classifies three factors correctly, with some reasons given
2 marks: Classifies two factors correctly, with limited reasons
1 mark: Identifies at least one factor as a determinant of health
markerNotes: Full marks need each factor placed in one category, with a reason tied to that factor rather than a general description of determinants.
Accept a different category only with a sound reason, such as smoking also reflecting the social conditions that shape it.
A correct category with no reason cannot reach the top row.
commonStudentErrors: Places household income under health behaviours, confusing a social circumstance with a personal choice.
Classifies air pollution as a health behaviour because residents could move house.
Uses the term biomedical factor for household income or other social features.

sampleAnswers.answer: Household income is a socioeconomic characteristic, because it shapes access to housing, nutritious food and health services. Air pollution near a major road is an environmental factor, since it affects the air residents breathe every day. Regular smoking is a health behaviour, which is a choice individuals can change, although it is shaped by social and economic conditions. A family history of heart disease is a biomedical factor, because it relates to a person's physical make-up and inherited risk, which cannot easily be changed. Together these show the range of determinants of health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Places all four factors in the correct category with a reason for each, which meets the 4-mark row. The closing sentence links the factors back to the determinants of health.

sampleAnswers.answer: Household income is a socioeconomic characteristic because it affects what people can afford. Regular smoking is a health behaviour.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies two factors correctly with limited reasons, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Air pollution is one of the factors that can affect health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a factor that influences health without classifying it, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Discuss how the determinants of health interact to affect the health of a population group, and where inequities in health exist.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A population group in an outer suburb has a high proportion of low-income households, limited public transport and high rates of smoking. Some residents also report difficulty getting a regular appointment with a general practitioner.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how the determinants of health interact to affect the population group, with sustained links to the scenario and a judgement about where inequities exist
5 marks: Discusses how several determinants affect the population group, with relevant links to the scenario
4 marks: Explains how two determinants affect the health of the population group, with some links to the scenario
3 marks: Describes a determinant of health and its effect on residents, with a limited link to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a determinant of health, with a basic link to the scenario
1 mark: Identifies a factor that may influence the health of residents
markerNotes: Strong answers show the determinants interacting, for example low income limiting transport and food choices, rather than listing them.
Credit a judgement on where inequities cluster in the scenario and what could reduce them, such as affordable housing or transport.
Individual choices such as smoking are credited only when linked to the social conditions that shape them.
commonStudentErrors: Lists the determinants in categories without explaining how any of them interact.
Treats smoking as a purely individual choice, ignoring the social and economic conditions that shape it.
Treats any difference between groups as an inequity, without asking whether the difference is avoidable and unfair.

sampleAnswers.answer: The determinants of health interact, so a single factor rarely explains the health of a population group. Low income is a socioeconomic characteristic that limits housing choices, healthy food and private transport, which increases exposure to other risks. Limited public transport makes it harder to reach services and jobs, and it can increase isolation. High smoking rates are health behaviours shaped by stress, peer norms and social settings, so they are not simply individual choices. Difficulty booking a regular general practitioner reflects limited service access, which compounds the other determinants because illness is detected late. Biomedical factors, such as high blood pressure, are then more likely to develop into serious conditions. Inequities exist where these determinants cluster in disadvantaged areas, and they can be reduced through affordable housing, improved transport, smoking cessation programs and better access to primary care.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses how several determinants interact to affect the population group, with sustained links to the scenario and a judgement about where inequities exist, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Low income and limited public transport make it harder for residents to reach healthy food and services. High smoking rates are a health behaviour, and the scenario shows these determinants affecting the population group. Some residents cannot book a regular doctor, which adds to the problem.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how two determinants affect the population group, with some links to the scenario, which meets the 4-mark row. It does not discuss several determinants interacting, so the 5-mark row is not met.

sampleAnswers.answer: Low income in this suburb is a socioeconomic characteristic that may affect health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a determinant of health with a basic link to the scenario, which meets the 2-mark row.

subTopics.name: What are young people’s meanings of health?

dotPoints.description: Explore across generations aspects of young people’s lives that make them similar and different to the young people of previous generations

prompts.question: Describe two aspects of young people's lives that differ from those of young people in previous generations, using the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class is interviewing a parent and a grandparent about their own teenage years, then comparing the answers with their own lives today.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes two aspects of young people's lives that differ from previous generations, with a clear explanation of how each affects health or wellbeing
3 marks: Describes two differences between generations, with a limited link to health
2 marks: Describes one difference between young people today and previous generations
1 mark: Identifies a similarity or difference between generations
markerNotes: Full marks need two differences, each explained for its effect on health or wellbeing, not only described.
Credit an aspect such as access to technology, education or independence, provided the generational difference is clear.
Stating that life was simply better or worse in the past earns no credit without evidence of how it differed.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the lives of young people today without saying how they differ from previous generations.
Gives a difference but no effect on health or wellbeing.
Presents a generational difference as a fact about every young person, without qualifying it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people today spend much more time using digital technology, such as smartphones and social media, than young people in previous generations did. This exposes them to constant online comparison and contact with peers, which can affect their mental health and sleep. Young people in previous generations often left school and entered the workforce earlier, whereas many young people today stay in education or at home for longer, which can delay independence and shape financial stress. Some aspects are different, but others remain similar, such as the importance of family and friends for wellbeing in every generation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two differences and explains how each affects health or wellbeing, which meets the 4-mark row. The closing sentence notes what has stayed similar across generations.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people today use smartphones and social media much more than young people in previous generations did.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one difference between the generations, which meets the 2-mark row. A second difference with a link to health would reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people today have different lives from their grandparents.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a difference between the generations without describing it, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Compare the lives of young people today with those of young people in previous generations, and show how one difference could affect the health of young people.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A health class is comparing the daily routines of Year 11 students with those of their grandparents at the same age, including school, work, transport and use of technology.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Compares the lives of young people today and in previous generations in detail, showing how one difference affects health with clear reasoning
4 marks: Compares two aspects of young people's lives across generations, with a link to health
3 marks: Compares one aspect of young people's lives across generations, with a limited link to health
2 marks: Describes one aspect of young people's lives today or in the past
1 mark: Identifies a similarity or difference between generations
markerNotes: Strong answers compare the same aspect in both generations, such as daily technology use, rather than describing each generation separately.
A difference earns credit for health only when it is explained as affecting sleep, stress or mental health.
A similarity counts only when it is used in the comparison, not as a stand-alone observation.
commonStudentErrors: Describes life today and life in the past in two separate paragraphs without comparing them.
Claims that young people in previous generations had no pressures or health concerns.
Links technology use to health without explaining the effect on sleep, stress or mental health.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people today and young people in previous generations share some similar pressures, such as school expectations and the need to build friendships. However, their daily experiences are different. Many young people today use smartphones and social media for much of the day, which exposes them to constant comparison with peers and can disrupt sleep. In previous generations, young people had fewer screens and more face-to-face contact, which meant less exposure to online comparison. Because sleep and social pressure both affect mental health, this difference can shape how well young people manage stress today. Mental health is affected by the amount of time spent online, so the difference matters for the health of young people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares the same aspect across both generations in detail and explains how the difference affects sleep and mental health, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people today use social media much more than young people in previous generations did, which may affect their sleep.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares one aspect of young people's lives across generations with a limited link to health, which meets the 3-mark row. A second aspect compared would strengthen the answer.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people today and in the past both go to school.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a similarity between the generations without comparing it or linking it to health, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Investigate the meanings of health for young people (creating a research question; developing a method(s) to collect data; considering how the determinants of health impact on a young person’s meaning of health; analysing the different ways young people define what is important to their own health; discussing ethical considerations; discussing validity, reliability and credibility of data collection; presenting findings and drawing conclusions; identifying further research questions that could be explored)

prompts.question: Construct a research question and one data collection method for investigating the meanings of health for young people.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 student wants to find out how classmates define health and what matters most to their own wellbeing.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Constructs a focused research question and a suitable data collection method, with clear detail on how the data answers the question
3 marks: Constructs a research question and a data collection method, with limited detail
2 marks: States a research question OR a data collection method, with basic detail
1 mark: Identifies a topic that could be investigated about health
markerNotes: Full marks need a research question that is focused and answerable, and a method that would collect data to answer it.
Credit a method that matches the question, such as a survey with open responses, and explains how the data will be analysed.
A broad topic with no question or method earns only the 1-mark row.
commonStudentErrors: Writes a question that a survey cannot answer, such as one about the cause of a health condition.
Names a method, such as a survey, without saying what data it will collect.
Offers a question that asks for yes or no answers, which limits the meanings of health students can describe.

sampleAnswers.answer: A suitable research question is: How do Year 11 students describe the meanings of health that matter most to young people, and what factors shape those views? The data collection method is a short anonymous survey with closed questions on common aspects of health and open questions asking students to describe, in their own words, what health means to them. The survey is given to a random sample of Year 11 students, which provides data from several classes. Open responses can reveal the reasons behind the meanings of health that students give.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Constructs a focused research question and a method that collects the data needed to answer it, with clear detail on how the open responses help, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The research question is: What does health mean to young people?
sampleAnswers.feedback: States a research question without a data collection method, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people's health could be studied.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a topic that could be investigated, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Evaluate the ethical considerations, and the validity, reliability and credibility, of the survey described in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student surveys 40 classmates online about what health means to them. The survey asks for each student's name, age and postcode, and it is open for two days. Some responses are only one word, and the student plans to publish the results on a social media page.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Evaluates the ethical considerations, validity, reliability and credibility of the survey with sustained judgement, weighing its strengths and limits against the scenario
5 marks: Evaluates several ethical considerations and at least two of validity, reliability and credibility, with a clear judgement
4 marks: Discusses at least one ethical consideration and one measure of data quality, with some links to the scenario
3 marks: Describes an ethical or data quality issue with a limited link to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a privacy or sample issue in the survey
1 mark: Identifies a feature of the survey
markerNotes: Strong answers judge the survey, for example by stating that publishing identifying details is not acceptable, rather than listing criteria.
Credit a student who separates validity, whether the survey measures meanings of health, from reliability, whether it would give the same results again.
Ethical points for participants under 18, including parental or guardian consent, carry more weight than a general mention of privacy.
commonStudentErrors: Uses validity and reliability as interchangeable terms.
Mentions consent only as a general courtesy, without noting the need for parent or guardian consent for participants under 18.
Says the survey is valid because 40 students completed it, without judging whether it measures what it intends.

sampleAnswers.answer: The survey raises several ethical considerations. Because it involves young people under 18, it needs informed consent from a parent or guardian as well as the student's own agreement, and participation should be voluntary. Asking for names and postcodes reduces privacy, and publishing results on social media could identify individuals, which breaches confidentiality. The validity of the data is limited because the survey may not measure the meanings of health students actually hold, especially when one-word answers give little depth. Reliability is also questionable, since a two-day window and a sample of 40 classmates would not necessarily produce the same findings if the survey were repeated with another group. Credibility is weakened by the lack of a clear method for analysing the data and by peer influence among friends who answer together. The data may still give a useful starting point, but overall the survey has limited credibility and needs redesign, with anonymous responses, a longer collection period and a wider, more representative sample before its conclusions are shared.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Evaluates the ethical considerations and the validity, reliability and credibility of the data with a clear judgement, weighing the strengths and limits against the scenario, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The survey raises ethical considerations, such as consent and privacy, because it asks for names and postcodes. The sample of 40 classmates is small, so the findings may not be reliable for other young people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses an ethical consideration and a measure of data quality with links to the scenario, which meets the 4-mark row. It does not evaluate validity or credibility with a judgement, so the 5-mark row is not met.

sampleAnswers.answer: Asking for names and postcodes is a privacy concern.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a privacy issue in the survey, which meets the 2-mark row.

subTopics.name: What key issues affect the health of young people and how can they protect and promote good health?

dotPoints.description: Examine the health status of young people, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people, using Australia’s Health and other health reports, graphs and tables (what are the trends in key health issues?; what are the causes and protective factors of key health issues?; how do the determinants of health affect health-related behaviours?)

prompts.question: Extract two trends from the table for young people, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A health report includes a table showing the proportion of young people reporting high psychological distress at two survey points. The proportion rose for young people overall, and the rise was larger for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Extracts two accurate trends for both groups, with the direction of each change clearly stated
2 marks: Extracts one accurate trend from the table
1 mark: Identifies a group or measure shown in the table
markerNotes: Full marks need two trends, one for young people overall and one comparing the two groups, each stated with its direction.
Accept wording such as increased or rose, provided the direction of change is read correctly from the table.
An explanation of why the trend occurred is not asked for and earns no extra marks.
commonStudentErrors: Gives an explanation of why distress increased, which the question does not ask for.
Reports the level of distress as a fixed figure rather than the change between the survey points.
Says the gap between the two groups narrowed, which reverses the trend shown in the table.

sampleAnswers.answer: The table shows that the proportion of young people reporting high psychological distress increased between the two survey points. The rise was larger for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people than for young people overall, so the health status gap between the two groups widened. These are two trends in the data for this health issue.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Extracts two accurate trends for both groups and states the direction of each, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Psychological distress rose for young people overall between the two survey points.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Extracts one accurate trend from the table, which meets the 2-mark row. A second trend comparing the two groups would reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The table shows psychological distress in young people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the measure and group shown in the table without stating a trend, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse the causes and protective factors of the health issue shown in the table, and how the determinants of health affect related health behaviours.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Young people in the table report high psychological distress, and many also report poor sleep and low levels of physical activity. Several also report a strong sense of connection to family and community.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the causes and protective factors of psychological distress, and how determinants of health shape related health behaviours, with sustained use of the scenario
5 marks: Analyses causes and protective factors, with relevant links between determinants of health and health behaviours
4 marks: Explains one cause or protective factor, with some link to a determinant of health
3 marks: Describes a cause or protective factor of distress, with a limited link to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a cause or protective factor, with a basic link to the scenario
1 mark: Identifies a health behaviour shown in the scenario
markerNotes: Strong answers analyse how a cause, such as poor sleep or financial stress, sits within the determinants of health rather than naming causes alone.
Protective factors should be linked to the scenario, such as connection to family and community, to earn the top rows.
Cultural connection is credited as a protective factor for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people, without treating the group as a deficit.
commonStudentErrors: Lists causes of distress without showing how they link to sleep or physical activity.
Treats poor sleep as the cause of distress and never considers that the two may reinforce each other.
Describes Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people as more likely to be distressed, without analysing the social conditions behind any difference.

sampleAnswers.answer: Psychological distress in young people has several causes, including academic pressure, social media comparison, financial stress and family conflict, which together increase the risk of anxiety and low mood. The scenario shows that poor sleep and low physical activity accompany the distress, and these health behaviours both reflect and worsen mental health. The determinants of health shape these behaviours: a young person with limited income may not afford sport, and one living with stress at home may struggle to sleep. Protective factors include strong family support, friendships, early access to help and a sense of belonging to a community. The scenario's reported connection to family and community is a protective factor, because it buffers stress and encourages help-seeking. For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people, cultural connection and kinship can be a strong protective factor, although they may also face additional stressors such as discrimination. Analysing these causes and protective factors together shows that mental health is shaped by social and economic conditions, not individual choices alone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the causes and protective factors of distress, and how the determinants of health shape related health behaviours, with sustained use of the scenario, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Academic pressure and social media comparison are causes of psychological distress, and they add to the stress of young people with less family support. Poor sleep is a health behaviour that often accompanies the distress.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains a cause and links it to a determinant of health, which meets the 4-mark row. The answer does not show how the health behaviours and protective factors interact, so it stops short of the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Family support is a protective factor against psychological distress.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a protective factor with a basic link to the scenario, which meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Research ONE health-related issue for young people (what is the nature of the issue?; what does the data tell us?; why is this an issue?; what are the protective factors to prevent the issue?; what strategies are currently in place to improve the health of young people?; what new strategies would be most effective to improve young people’s health?; what further research questions could be explored to build understanding and advocacy?)

prompts.question: Identify the nature of this health issue for young people, and two protective factors that help prevent it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student researching a health-related issue for young people chooses poor mental health, which includes persistent anxiety, low mood and difficulty coping with school pressure.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Identifies the nature of the issue with accurate detail, and two relevant protective factors that help prevent it
2 marks: Identifies the nature of the issue, or one protective factor, with some detail
1 mark: Identifies a health-related issue for young people
markerNotes: Full marks need the issue described by its nature, such as its signs or symptoms, plus two protective factors that help prevent it.
A protective factor must reduce the risk of the issue, not just describe a related circumstance.
Naming a broad topic such as youth health earns the 1-mark row only.
commonStudentErrors: Names an issue such as mental health without describing its nature or signs.
Lists a risk factor, such as academic pressure, as a protective factor.
Gives two protective factors without linking them to the issue they help prevent.

sampleAnswers.answer: For this research, the issue is poor mental health among young people, shown by persistent anxiety, low mood and difficulty coping with school and social pressure. Two protective factors are strong family and peer support, and early access to a school counsellor or mental health service, which help young people recognise and manage problems before they escalate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the nature of the issue with accurate detail and two relevant protective factors that help prevent it, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The issue is poor mental health among young people, such as anxiety and low mood.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the nature of the issue with some detail, which meets the 2-mark row. Two protective factors would reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A health issue for young people is poor mental health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a health-related issue without describing its nature, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Justify which new strategy would be most effective to improve the health of young people, with reference to the protective factors for this issue.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A school survey found that many students feel stressed about exams, and that students who have a trusted adult to talk to report better wellbeing. The school is considering peer support training or a mental health literacy program taught in class time.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies the most effective strategy with sustained reasoning, weighing both strategies against the protective factors and the nature of the issue, and identifies further research questions
5 marks: Justifies the most effective strategy with relevant reasoning that links it to the protective factors
4 marks: Justifies a strategy with some reasoning about its effect on young people
3 marks: Describes a strategy and how it could help young people, with a limited link to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a strategy for young people with a basic reason
1 mark: Identifies a health-related issue or strategy in the scenario
markerNotes: Strong answers reach a clear judgement on which strategy is more effective and justify it against the survey evidence, rather than describing both.
Credit a student who notes that a strategy's effect should be evaluated, such as through before-and-after wellbeing measures.
A justification that ignores the protective factors in the scenario cannot reach the top row.
commonStudentErrors: Describes both strategies without deciding which one is more effective.
Justifies the choice as better without any link to the survey findings.
Treats a classroom program as certain to change behaviour, without noting that ongoing support is needed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Peer support training is the most effective of the two strategies being considered, because it builds the protective factors the survey identified, namely trusted relationships and early help-seeking. Peer support places a trained student in a position to listen, refer and encourage others, which can reach young people before stress becomes serious. A mental health literacy program taught in class time is also valuable, because it teaches students to recognise the signs of mental health problems and where to seek help. However, it reaches every student in the same way and may not change behaviour without ongoing support. Peer support is therefore the stronger choice, since the survey links wellbeing to trusted relationships and the strategy strengthens those relationships directly. Its effectiveness should still be checked, so the school could track wellbeing before and after the program. Further research questions could ask whether peer support improves help-seeking among young people who rarely talk to adults.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies the most effective strategy by weighing both strategies against the protective factors and the nature of the issue, and identifies further research questions, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Peer support training is more effective because trusted relationships are protective factors that the survey identifies. A mental health literacy program is also useful, but it may not reach the young people who are most at risk.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies a strategy with some reasoning about its effect on young people, which meets the 4-mark row. Both strategies are not weighed against the nature of the issue, so the 5-mark row is not met.

sampleAnswers.answer: Peer support training would help students talk to someone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a strategy for young people with a basic reason, which meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Analyse how the skills for strengthening the individual can protect and enhance the health and wellbeing of themselves and others using the health issue researched (self-efficacy; health literacy; help-seeking behaviours; problem-solving; resilience; coping strategies; sense of purpose; ethical behaviour; connectedness)

prompts.question: Describe two skills for strengthening the individual that could help a Year 11 student manage stress, using the health issue Mei researched.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Mei, a Year 11 student, has researched stress and anxiety among students in her year. She found that many classmates keep their worries private and do not ask teachers or school counsellors for help until a problem becomes serious.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two skills for strengthening the individual, with sound links to how each protects a student facing stress
2 marks: Describes one skill for strengthening the individual and links it to the health issue researched
1 mark: Identifies a relevant skill or support action
markerNotes: Strong answers name two distinct skills, such as self-efficacy and help-seeking behaviours, and describe what each involves rather than only naming it.
Each skill should be tied to the stress and anxiety Mei researched, so the answer shows how the skill protects the student's health.
Brief, precise description earns full marks; length on its own does not.
commonStudentErrors: Names skills such as resilience without describing what they involve.
Describes a skill in general terms without linking it to the health issue researched.

sampleAnswers.answer: Self-efficacy is a student's belief that they can carry out a behaviour, such as asking for help, when stress builds up. Mei could encourage classmates to build it through small successes, a practical step in stress management. Help-seeking behaviours are the actions students take to get support, such as speaking to a trusted teacher or counsellor. Connectedness and peer support make these actions easier.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two skills are described clearly, and each is linked to students who keep stress private. Connectedness and peer support extend the answer without padding it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Self-efficacy is a student's belief that they can manage a problem such as stress, so they are more willing to act. Students who lack it may avoid asking for help.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One skill is described with a link to stress, which meets the 2-mark row. A second skill is missing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Students should talk to a teacher when they are stressed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A support action is identified, but no skill is described or linked to the health issue.

prompts.question: Discuss how Tom's self-efficacy, sense of purpose and connectedness could help him protect the health and wellbeing of his friends, using the health issue he researched.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Tom, a Year 11 student, has researched sleep problems and screen use among teenagers. He has noticed that some friends stay up late gaming, and he is worried that they are missing out on rest and feeling irritable at school.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how Tom's self-efficacy, sense of purpose and connectedness could work together to protect the health and wellbeing of his friends, with sustained and relevant links to the sleep issue researched
5 marks: Discusses how two of these skills could protect friends' health, with relevant links to the issue
4 marks: Discusses one or two skills in relation to protecting the health of others, with some reasoning
3 marks: Describes a skill for strengthening the individual and makes a limited link to others
2 marks: Identifies a skill and makes a general link to health
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: The top row needs a discussion that weighs how the skills work together, not a list of skills followed by a list of benefits to friends.
Links to others should be specific, such as how a changed habit could affect a friend's concentration, mood or sleep.
Strong answers acknowledge limits, such as peer resistance, and explain how Tom could respond to them.
commonStudentErrors: Lists several skills without explaining how any of them protects other people's health.
Treats the skills as guaranteed to change friends' behaviour, with no acknowledgement of resistance.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tom's self-efficacy is the starting point. If he believes he can influence his friends' habits, he is more likely to raise the issue and suggest a change, such as a phone-free hour before bed. Sleep hygiene, such as a regular bedtime and dimmed screens, gives him practical changes he can model rather than only lecture. His sense of purpose also matters, because a clear goal, such as playing well in the next season, gives his friends a reason to change habits they might otherwise dismiss. Connectedness adds further strength, since friends who trust Tom are more likely to listen to him than to a teacher or parent. The protection is not guaranteed. Some friends may resist, so Tom must respect their choices while still speaking up. Peer support works best when it is shared, so he could invite a few friends to try the change together. Over time, a group that sleeps better and is less irritable at school is better placed to protect its own health and wellbeing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Each skill is explained and applied to friends' health, and the answer weighs the limits of peer influence. The sleep focus connects directly to the researched issue.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tom's self-efficacy could help him raise sleep problems with friends and suggest changes such as a phone-free hour before bed. A sense of purpose could also motivate them. Friends who trust him may listen more than they would to a teacher.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Skills are linked to friends' health with some reasoning, but the discussion is brief and does not weigh the limits.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tom has self-efficacy and connectedness, so he can talk to friends about sleep and health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A skill is named and a general link to health is made, but there is little discussion.

dotPoints.description: Reflect on their own personal health and health behaviours and indicate courses of action for improved health and wellbeing

prompts.question: Describe two health behaviours shown in Jordan's diary that could affect his personal health and wellbeing.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Jordan, a Year 11 student, kept a one-week health diary. It shows about five hours of screen time on most nights, sleep of under seven hours on two nights, a sugary drink on most school days and no physical activity at weekends. He wrote that he often feels tired in class.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two health behaviours from Jordan's diary and explains how each could affect his personal health
2 marks: Describes one health behaviour from the diary and links it to a possible effect on health
1 mark: Identifies a relevant behaviour from the diary
markerNotes: Strong answers choose two behaviours clearly shown in the diary and explain a likely effect on health or wellbeing for each.
Credit links that use the scenario's figures, such as five hours of screen time, rather than generic statements about health.
Behaviours should be linked to an effect, not simply listed.
commonStudentErrors: Lists every behaviour in the diary without choosing two or linking either to an effect on health.
States that screen time is unhealthy without explaining how it affects sleep, activity or health.

sampleAnswers.answer: Jordan's screen time of about five hours on most nights is a sedentary behaviour that can delay sleep and reduce time for physical activity. His short sleep on two nights is another of his health behaviours that can affect his concentration and mood. Together with a sugary drink on most school days, these habits could weaken his personal health and add to the tiredness he reports in class.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two health behaviours from the diary are described, and each is linked to a likely effect on personal health. The figures from the scenario are used accurately.

sampleAnswers.answer: Jordan's screen time is a sedentary behaviour that can delay sleep. Short sleep may leave him tired at school.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One behaviour is linked to a likely effect, but the second is not described. This is a 2-mark response.

sampleAnswers.answer: Jordan has little sleep and drinks sugary drinks.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A behaviour from the diary is identified without an explanation of its effect.

prompts.question: Recommend two courses of action Jordan could take to improve his personal health and wellbeing, linking each to a behaviour in his diary.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: After reviewing his diary, Jordan wants changes that fit the school term. He works part-time on weekday evenings, plays in a Saturday sport team and has limited money to spend on food and drinks.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Recommends two realistic courses of action for Jordan, each clearly linked to a behaviour in his diary and explained in terms of improved health and wellbeing
4 marks: Recommends two courses of action linked to the diary, with some explanation of how they improve health
3 marks: Recommends one course of action that relates to a behaviour in the diary
2 marks: Suggests a general healthy-lifestyle action with limited link to the diary
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: The top row needs two realistic courses of action that suit Jordan's job, sport commitments and budget, rather than generic healthy-lifestyle advice.
Each recommendation should be tied to a specific behaviour from the diary, such as screen time before bed.
A brief reason, such as an expected effect on sleep or energy, is needed to reach full marks.
commonStudentErrors: Recommends actions that ignore Jordan's part-time job, sport commitments or limited money.
Gives generic advice such as eat healthy or exercise more without linking it to the diary.

sampleAnswers.answer: Jordan's first course of action is to set a goal of a screen-free hour before bed on school nights, which targets the sedentary behaviour and short sleep in his diary. Goal setting makes the change specific, and self-monitoring, such as logging his screen time each evening, shows whether it is working. The second course of action is a 20-minute walk before his Saturday game, which adds physical activity without extra cost or time. Both courses of action fit his part-time job and limited budget. Together they improve his health behaviours, personal health and wellbeing, and they build habits he can keep through the school term. Better sleep may also help his concentration in class, which is the tiredness he reports.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two courses of action are recommended, each tied to a behaviour in the diary and to Jordan's circumstances. The answer explains how each change improves health and wellbeing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Jordan could set a screen-free hour before bed, which would help with the screen time shown in his diary.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One relevant course of action is linked to the diary, which meets the 3-mark row. A second course is needed for more marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Jordan should eat healthier food and sleep more.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Generic advice is given with no link to the diary or to Jordan's circumstances.

subTopics.name: What are the opportunities for improving and promoting young people’s health?

dotPoints.description: Examine how young people advocate for their own and others’ health using various sources considering past, current and future advocacy and the role of individuals within their communities

prompts.question: Describe how each of the three sources shows young people advocating for health, and whether the advocacy is past, current or future.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class is studying how young people advocate for health. Their three sources are an earlier school newsletter article about students who gathered signatures for refill stations, a current post by a youth group asking for free sunscreen at the school canteen, and a student plan for a community forum on mental health next year.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes how young people advocate for their own and others' health in each source, with sustained links to past, current and future advocacy
3 marks: Describes advocacy in at least two sources, with some reference to whether it is past, current or future
2 marks: Describes advocacy in one source with limited reference to its time frame
1 mark: Identifies a relevant example of advocacy
markerNotes: Full marks need all three sources described, each placed in time as past, current or future advocacy.
Strong answers show advocacy both for the young people's own health and for the health of others.
Naming the source is not enough; the answer must say what the source shows about advocacy.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the sources without saying whether the advocacy is past, current or future.
Treats advocacy as only individual action and ignores the groups or communities involved.

sampleAnswers.answer: The earlier newsletter article shows past advocacy, because students gathered signatures to ask for refill stations. This is self-advocacy, as young people speak up for their own health and that of other students. The youth group's current post shows present advocacy for others, as it asks the canteen to provide free sunscreen to protect every student. The student plan for a community forum on mental health shows future advocacy, since it sets out how young people intend to raise concerns with local decision-makers. Across the three sources, young people advocate both for themselves and for others, which is a form of community action.
sampleAnswers.feedback: All three sources are described, and each is placed in time as past, current or future advocacy. The answer shows advocacy for both self and others.

sampleAnswers.answer: The newsletter article shows past advocacy by students asking for refill stations, which helps their own health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One source is described with a time frame, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The sources show young people speaking up about health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The sources are described in general terms without a clear example of advocacy or time frame.

prompts.question: Examine how past and current advocacy by young people could shape their future advocacy for health, and what individuals within their communities can do to make it effective.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional youth group ran a petition about healthy food at the local sports club and is now planning a campaign on sleep and screen use. Its members want to know how that earlier work can guide future advocacy, and what individual students can do to strengthen it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Examines how past and current advocacy could shape future advocacy for young people's health, with sustained reasoning about the role of individuals within communities
5 marks: Examines how earlier advocacy could shape future advocacy, with relevant reference to individuals and communities
4 marks: Examines how advocacy could be used in the future, with some reference to earlier work or to individuals
3 marks: Describes a way young people could advocate for health, with limited reference to past or current work
2 marks: Identifies a relevant form of advocacy with general links to the scenario
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Full marks need reasoning about how past and current advocacy shape the future, not a separate description of each.
The role of individuals should be specific, such as speaking at a meeting, recruiting peers or mentoring younger members.
Strong answers recognise that changing habits, such as screen use, is harder to advocate for than a clear environmental change.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the petition and the campaign without explaining how one shapes the other.
Gives advice to the youth group in general terms that could apply to any campaign.

sampleAnswers.answer: Past advocacy shapes future advocacy because it shows what young people can achieve. The petition shows that a clear request backed by signatures is one way young people can put a health issue on the agenda. Current advocacy on sleep and screen use builds on that experience, but it has a harder target because habits are personal and sometimes difficult to change. To make future advocacy effective, young people can draw on health promotion evidence, pick a clear and achievable goal and communicate it through the channels their peers use. Individuals within their communities also matter. A student who speaks at a council meeting, recruits friends or mentors younger members can extend the campaign beyond its founders. Communities can support this by giving young people a place at the table, so that advocacy becomes a lasting part of local decisions rather than a single event. Strong civic engagement of this kind keeps the campaign alive.

sampleAnswers.answer: The elbow is a synovial joint, a hinge joint formed by the humerus, radius and ulna that allows flexion and extension. When Priya lowers the bag under control, the biceps brachii performs an eccentric muscle contraction, lengthening while still producing tension.

sampleAnswers.answer: The quadriceps are the agonist for knee extension, so they are the prime mover in the forward swing. This group of four muscles on the front of the thigh attaches to the tibia through the patellar tendon, and as it shortens it straightens the knee. This is a concentric muscle contraction that produces the force to drive the ball. The hamstrings, on the back of the thigh, are the antagonist, because they flex the knee. During the forward swing they lengthen while the quadriceps shorten, so they relax to allow the extension to happen. As the leg reaches full extension, the hamstrings contract eccentrically to slow and control the movement, which protects the knee from excessive strain. This muscle relationship means the two muscle groups work in opposition, producing smooth and controlled movement rather than simply throwing the leg through the kick.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first principle is to keep the centre of mass of the load close to the body. When the box is held away from the body, its weight acts further from the lower back, which increases the turning force, or moment, on the lumbar spine. Holding the box close shortens this moment arm and reduces the strain the back muscles must counteract. The second principle is to use a wide base of support and bend at the hips and knees rather than the back. A wider stance lowers the centre of mass and increases stability, while the large muscles of the thighs and buttocks, working through the hip and knee joints, generate the force to lift the load. Together these biomechanical principles support safe movement: the worker lifts with the legs, keeps the spine straight and avoids twisting, because twisting adds rotational force to a load that is already heavy.

sampleAnswers.answer: A red blood cell returning from the body enters the right atrium through the vena cava, passes into the right ventricle, and is pumped through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. sampleAnswers.answer: Endurance training is likely to lower Mia's resting heart rate and increase her stroke volume. A larger stroke volume means the left ventricle pumps more blood with each beat, so the heart does not need to beat as often to deliver the same blood flow. Her resting heart rate falls because the parasympathetic nervous system slows the heart more strongly at rest, and the larger stroke volume means fewer beats are needed. Training also increases her blood volume, particularly plasma volume, which fills the ventricles more completely and supports a larger stroke volume. Cardiac output, the product of heart rate and stroke volume, can stay stable at rest while the heart works less, and during exercise it can rise further to meet the demand for oxygen from the muscles. These changes improve the efficiency of the cardiovascular system, because the heart delivers the same blood flow with less effort.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the first few seconds, the ATP-PCr system supplies most of the ATP, because phosphocreatine is broken down immediately to resynthesise ATP without oxygen. Fatigue in the final 20 seconds is caused mainly by hydrogen ions accumulating in the muscle, which interfere with contraction, together with depletion of phosphocreatine and glycogen. Fatigue therefore reflects the limits of the energy systems rather than a single cause, and the falling power reflects the decline in the glycolytic and phosphocreatine supply as the effort proceeds.

prompts.question: Compare aerobic and anaerobic training for an individual marathon runner and for a group sports player, including a contemporary method of training suited to each.

sampleAnswers.answer: The individual runner's aerobic training uses oxygen to release energy from carbohydrate and fat during long, steady efforts, which builds endurance and improves the heart's capacity to deliver oxygen to working muscles. The group sports player's anaerobic training relies on the ATP-PCr and glycolytic systems for short, intense bursts, building power and the ability to recover between efforts. Both athletes use both energy systems, but in different proportions, so their weekly sessions look very different. The runner's training is mostly continuous, while the player's is mostly intermittent, which is why each needs a different plan. A contemporary method of training suited to the runner is steady running monitored by wearable heart rate monitors, which keeps effort in the aerobic zone. For the player, high-intensity interval training with timed recovery matches the stop-start demands of the game.
